summary: This informational document examines problems that arise when providers share one IPv4 address among many subscribers due to address exhaustion. It looks at several emerging solutions and their effects on applications. It is analysis, not a protocol.

eli5.summary: When houses must share one phone number, some things break. This lists the troubles that come up when many users share one internet address.

questions: how do you trace a user behind cgn
subtitle: What breaks, and for whom, when many subscribers share a single public IPv4 address.

tldr.problem: IPv4 address allocations from IANA were completed on February 3, 2011, so providers can no longer give every subscriber their own public IPv4 address and are turning to shared addressing.
tldr.mechanism: The memo catalogs the issues common to all address sharing approaches, such as CGN, Dual-Stack Lite, NAT64 and port-range schemes, and says which issues hit the deploying provider and which hit third parties like content providers and law enforcement.
tldr.outcome: Sharing breaks or degrades port-based services, ICMP, geo-location, abuse handling and traceability. The memo says deploying IPv6 is the only perennial way to ease the pressure.

today: RFC 6269 is an Informational RFC published in June 2011, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is an analysis of issues, not a protocol, and its solution-specific references such as Port Control Protocol and Dual-Stack Lite were still works in progress when it was written.

sections.title: Why Addresses Are Being Shared
sections.content:
Allocations of IPv4 addresses from IANA were completed on February 3, 2011, and allocations from the Regional Internet Registries were expected to finish around a year later. Service providers therefore face a world where they cannot give each subscriber a public IPv4 address. Several solutions based on shared IPv4 addressing are emerging.

This memo does not pick a solution. It collects the issues common to all of them, including application failures, additional service monitoring complexity and new security vulnerabilities. Solution-specific discussion is out of scope. It states that deploying IPv6 is the only perennial way to ease pressure on the public IPv4 pool without address sharing, and that more IPv6 traffic should mean fewer concurrent IPv4 sessions per subscriber, so more subscribers per shared address.
sections.eli5: There are not enough internet addresses left, so providers want to make many homes share one. Sharing causes problems, and this note lists them.

sections.title: Kinds of Address Sharing
sections.content:
Today a home or small business usually gets one public IPv4 address on its CPE (Customer Premises Equipment), and a NAT in that device translates private RFC 1918 addresses to it. The new proposals multiplex many subscribers over fewer addresses. Appendix A sorts them into two classes.

CGN-based solutions put a NAPT function, called Carrier Grade NAT or Large Scale NAT, in the provider network. Subscribers get private addresses and the CGN pool of public addresses is smaller than the number of subscribers. NAT444 uses two layers of NAT, and Dual-Stack Lite uses a single layer. Port-range solutions avoid a CGN: several subscribers share one public address, and each is given a non-overlapping range of ports. Examples named are A+P, Port Range and Stateless Address Mapping.

The memo argues that the view from the outside is what matters, so most issues apply whichever approach is used. Unlike traditional NAT problems, which touched a single legal entity, these issues increasingly span several legal entities at once.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to share. Either a big switchboard hands out private numbers and connects calls, or each home gets its own slice of extension numbers on the same line.

sections.title: Port Allocation
sections.content:
For outgoing connections the source port is usually irrelevant, though in a port-range scheme it must fall inside the allocated range. For incoming connections the specific ports matter, because third parties use them to reach services run by subscribers. The number of subscribers per address depends on average ports per active subscriber and on how many are active at once. Ports in the TCP TIME-WAIT state, typically 4 minutes after a connection ends, still count toward usage.

Measurements cited in the memo show that average outgoing port use is far below the maximum, with a heavy tail of a few heavy users. Dynamic allocation from a central pool therefore lets more subscribers share an address than static division does, but it makes record keeping harder. Per-subscriber limits are needed so that a worm-infected device cannot exhaust the shared address for everyone.

Incoming ports are harder. Port forwarding by UPnP IGD or NAT-PMP assumes a publicly routable WAN address, so with a CGN the CPE and CGN must cooperate. Connections to well-known ports will not work in the general case, DNS SRV records help only for some protocols, and UDP-based service discovery breaks because unsolicited inbound UDP is dropped.
sections.eli5: A shared address has only so many numbered doors. Giving every home a fixed set wastes doors, but handing them out on demand makes it harder to remember who used which door, and visitors cannot find a home's usual door anymore.

sections.title: Impact on Applications and Protocols
sections.content:
Applications at risk include those that need inbound connections, carry addresses or ports in their payload (and so need an ALG), use fixed ports, assume an IP address identifies one host, or forbid concurrent connections from the same address. Protocols other than TCP, UDP and ICMP, such as SCTP, DCCP, RSVP and IPsec ESP, are not supported by the proposals to date.

ICMP has no port field, so replies and error messages need special handling, for example using the ICMP Identifier. Path MTU discovery suffers when hosts cache a wrong MTU, and a malicious ICMP Packet Too Big message advertising an MTU as low as 68 octets could be cached for every subscriber sharing the address. Only the first fragment carries port information, so fragments need special handling. Other items covered include TCP control block sharing, reverse DNS, load balancing, 6to4 transition mechanisms, single points of failure, keep-alives that shorten battery life, multicast and Mobile IP.
sections.eli5: Many programs assume one address means one computer. When many computers share an address, programs that make that assumption get confused, and some special kinds of messages cannot be delivered at all.

sections.title: Geo-location, Tracking and Traceability
sections.content:
A subscriber behind a CGN geo-locates to wherever the CGN prefix appears to be, often a different city, which degrades licensed-content restrictions, targeted advertising and proximity-based delivery. Counting unique users by unique IP address also becomes much less useful, so monitors along the chain must take the port into account.

Traceability is the sharpest problem. A legal request of the form source address plus time no longer identifies one subscriber. The memo describes two fixes: servers log the source port too, so a request can carry the source address, port and timestamp, which demands accurate time-keeping; or providers log destination addresses, which the memo calls inferior. Providers must retain mappings, typically for 6 to 12 months depending on the jurisdiction, which is a heavy volume of data. Pre-allocating groups of ports reduces the logging burden.
sections.eli5: If a whole street uses one phone number, the phone company cannot tell which house made a particular call unless somebody also wrote down which extension and what time.

sections.title: Security Issues from Sharing
sections.content:
The memo itself defines no protocol and creates no new security issues, but it describes several implications of sharing. Penalty boxes and CAPTCHA triggers that react to many requests from one address will punish innocent subscribers, and one user's failed logins can block others. Blacklists for spam or infected machines hit everyone behind the address, and address-based access control lists and some address-based signatures stop working.

Port randomization is weakened because the port space is smaller; allocating non-contiguous ranges can help. Providers should follow ingress filtering practice so that source addresses, or source ports in port-range schemes, are set correctly. The impact on IPsec should be evaluated, and providers should avoid blocking NAT traversal for protocols such as IKE.
sections.eli5: When many people share one address, blocking a troublemaker also blocks all the neighbors, and it is easier for bad guys to guess which door is open.
